claims.text: The relevant eutectic HEA has a fine lamellar microstructure with alternating ductile FCC and harder B2 phases.
The constituent phases differ in electrochemical nobility and oxide stability.
A protective oxide layer initially forms on the alloy at elevated temperature.
Eutectic phase boundaries and interlamellar interfaces are important sites controlling material behavior.
Electrochemical-potential differences at eutectic phase boundaries produce localized galvanic cells.
Mechanical sliding preferentially removes protective oxide from the more anodic phase near phase boundaries.
Mechanical removal of oxide exposes fresh, less-protected metal.
Exposed anodic regions undergo enhanced corrosion because of micro-galvanic coupling between the phases.
Localized corrosion further weakens the oxide scale and promotes additional mechanical damage.
Oxide removal and localized corrosion form a positive feedback loop that accelerates both wear and corrosion.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion produce a higher total degradation rate than either wear-only or corrosion-only exposure.
Simultaneous exposure produces deeper wear tracks than isolated wear exposure.
Simultaneous exposure produces greater corrosion-pit density than isolated corrosion exposure.
The proposed mechanism applies in the stated elevated-temperature range of approximately 450–650 °C.
Synergistic degradation is expected when the constituent phases have significantly different corrosion potentials and oxide stabilities.
Single-phase alloys or multiphase alloys with negligible electrochemical contrast will exhibit less synergistic degradation.
The acceleration factor depends on alloy composition, microstructural scale, and the severity of the corrosive and mechanical environments.
Failure of simultaneous exposure to exceed the additive effects of isolated wear and isolated corrosion is defined as falsifying the proposed synergy.

contradictions.description: The baseline calls for a wear-only sample under identical environmental conditions, but if those conditions include the same corrosive medium used during simultaneous exposure, that sample is not wear-only. The detailed experiment partly resolves this by matching only mechanical and temperature conditions for the wear control, leaving the baseline wording inconsistent.
